name: Colin Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a foam-cutting machine at a mattress plant. My vocational certificate taught safe blade changes and size checks. I like a clean, straight first panel; pulling tangled scrap from beneath a stopped cutter is dusty and slow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a grocery store, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn the normal operator wage, we have four months of expenses saved, and some similar plants are nearby. I never use AI tools; I trust my cut measurements and the setter's advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cutting crew a computer can print a mattress-size list, but it cannot feel a torn foam edge. We still need to check the first cut after changing the blade. I'd say the quiet AI picture sounds like our ordinary week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn about the normal rate for the foam cutter, my partner has regular grocery-store hours, and we have about four months of expenses saved. The mortgage and two school-age children are real costs, but we cover them and have some similar plants nearby. I can live with this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the foam cutter and measure the first mattress panel from each new roll. I'll show the younger operator how to stop the blade before clearing scraps, the way my vocational instructor showed me. I never use AI tools and see no reason to add one for a list that already works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My work is familiar and our wages are coming in. I'd rather spend my break with the family than watching a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad first cut look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A blade can drag soft foam and leave a sloping edge that looks square from above. I lay the panel on the measuring table before another roll is cut. A crooked mattress panel will not straighten itself inside the cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four months saved would cover a broken fridge or a short spell between jobs. We pay the mortgage from current wages and keep the children's school costs in the same monthly list. I don't spend the reserve on a better television.

say: A **size list** cannot catch a torn or crooked foam edge.
The crew still needs a **first-cut check** after each blade change.
think: Our **typical pay** and two regular wages cover current bills.
Four months of **savings** and some local plants give us a workable buffer.
do: **Keep** measuring the first mattress panel after each roll change.
**Show** a younger operator the safe blade stop during paid work.
feel: **Calm** about familiar work and current household money.
S0.quote: A crooked mattress panel will not straighten itself inside the cover.
fieldNote: Colin **never uses AI** and relies on blade checks he learned through vocational instruction.
His **four-month reserve** is for household gaps, while normal wages currently cover the mortgage and school costs.

steps.text: Keep cutting foam and measuring first mattress panels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may buy foam and write cut lists before robots move big rolls. The factory should show us the actual shift plan before calling the change a saving. I don't mind a new order sheet if nobody skips the first panel check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cutter is physical, so I expect to be needed for now. But a more efficient schedule could remove one of our paid changeover shifts; losing that regular wage would touch the mortgage. Four months saved buys time, not a reason to ignore the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor to post next month's paid changeover schedule and compare it with our last three slips. I'll keep cutting and checking first panels. If a required guarded blade-setting course is offered on paid time with a trainer at the stopped cutter, I'll attend, but I will not pay for an outside AI class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible lost shift, even while the machine stays familiar. I can check a rota before I have to use the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe blade training require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should make me lock the cutter, remove a dull blade and fit a replacement while the motor is isolated. I'd practise on a stopped machine and have the trainer sign me off. A demonstration across the room is not enough for a safe blade change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on the roster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare ordinary base hours, not the overtime a busy month can bring. If a paid changeover shift disappears, my partner and I would check whether grocery wages cover that part of the mortgage. I'd ask for the answer in writing.

say: **AI buying** may alter cut lists before robots lift foam rolls.
A **posted rota** should show paid changeover work and first-panel time.
think: My **physical cutter** still needs an operator for now.
One lost **base shift** could reduce mortgage money despite our reserve.
do: **Compare** posted paid changeover shifts with recent pay slips.
**Keep** cutting and inspecting first mattress panels.
**Attend** required paid blade-setting course if offered with stopped-machine instruction.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic reduction in regular paid hours.
S1.quote: A demonstration across the room is not enough for a safe blade change.
fieldNote: His **resistant style** favors a paid practical course on the physical cutter, not private AI study.
He checks **base hours** against actual slips before treating a schedule as a wage loss.

steps.text: Compare posted base changeover shifts with last three pay slips
Keep cutting and checking first mattress panels
Attend blade-setting course if required paid stopped-cutter place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI could write foam cut lists by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could load, cut and stack mattresses. We should ask the owner for a written plan for paid work. Family needs to know what is coming before the shifts vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the robots can handle the big foam rolls. I expect the cutting crew would lose most shifts, and my partner's grocery wage will not carry two children and the mortgage alone. Four months saved would disappear. I would be awake at night adding up the shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner this month for the robot date, notice and any remaining paid cutter roles. If a funded paid practical course in foam quality inspection is offered with a guarded place, I'll take it. If cutting hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local production jobs that pay enough regular wages and fit school pickup; after qualifying, I'll apply for posted local inspection work under the same conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I've stood at that cutter for years. A four-month reserve is no replacement for a year's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would quality training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection course would need a bad foam edge, a density test and practice beside a stopped cutter. A teacher should watch me reject a panel before it reaches the cover line. I won't reach around a moving blade to prove I learned anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What production job would you consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production fallback has to be a real local vacancy, with a safe task and base pay we can count on. My partner's grocery shifts cover afternoons, so a posting that ends at school pickup could work. I would compare the offered hours before applying.

say: **2028 thinking AI** writes cut lists before capable robots move foam around 2031.
The owner should publish **paid-role plans** and notice before cuts.
think: At **48**, I expect most cutter shifts could disappear.
Four months of **savings** and one grocery wage cannot carry the mortgage long.
do: **Ask** owner for written robot date, notice and paid roles.
**Attend** funded paid guarded foam-inspection training if offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local production or qualified inspection if cut, pay and pickup fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless bill calculations.
S2.quote: A four-month reserve is no replacement for a year's wage.
fieldNote: He expects **major cutter-hour loss** around 2031 and describes sleepless mortgage sums.
The **production fallback** and qualified inspection application both need real safe local posts, sufficient base pay and school-compatible hours.

steps.text: Ask owner for written robot date, notice and paid cutter roles
Attend foam inspection if funded paid guarded practical place offered
Apply for posted safe local production if hours cut, base pay and pickup fit
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours cut, pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 might plan the foam orders, but capable robots around 2034 would be the bigger change for the cutter. Five years could let us learn another workshop duty if the training is real and paid. I would ask local plants what they actually hire for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots reach the foam rolls. The children will be older, but I still expect to need a mortgage wage. Four months saved helps me refuse a bad offer, and I could put more away if full shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep cutting and pay extra mortgage principal from any offered paid overtime after bills. I'll ask the local upholstery shop whether it posts paid trim-machine apprenticeships with covered fees, a supervised safe place and a regular wage. If such a place is offered, I'll enrol; after qualifying, if my cutter hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local trim jobs only where base pay and travel time fit the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later shift loss, but I can check a real apprenticeship without leaving the wage we have. I prefer a trim-machine trainer showing me the blade to a screen explaining it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the upholstery apprenticeship need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trim shop would have to show the training wage, the guarded machine and who teaches each cut. I would not take a place that makes us pay fees while my mortgage comes due. I'd ask for its shift hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a trainee rate cover home costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job would have to be posted and close enough to get back for school pickup. A low trainee wage might work only if the shop states when a higher regular rate begins. If the figures do not cover bills, I stay on the cutter.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before capable robots handle foam around 2034.
A **paid workshop apprenticeship** could prepare a second machine duty if a real place opens.
think: At **51**, I still expect to need regular mortgage wages.
Four months of **savings** allows a careful offer check, not an unpaid course.
do: **Pay** extra mortgage principal from offered paid overtime after bills.
**Enrol** in trim apprenticeship if fees covered, guarded supervision and training pay sufficient.
**Apply** to posted safe local trim jobs if qualified, cutter hours cut, pay and travel fit.
feel: **Anxious** about later income risk with time to check real terms.
S3.quote: I prefer a trim-machine trainer showing me the blade to a screen explaining it.
fieldNote: He accepts **hands-on apprenticeship** conditionally, despite resisting AI, when the place pays and guarded instruction is real.
The **trim application** depends on qualification, reduced cutter hours, a local posting and sustainable base pay and travel.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from offered paid overtime after bills
Enrol in posted guarded trim apprenticeship if fees covered, training wage adequate and supervision offered
Apply for posted safe local trim role if qualified, hours cut, pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 could plan foam cuts, and capable robots around 2039 could lift and trim the panels. Ten years gives a worker time to learn a shop trade beside another person. It does not mean anyone owes me a job without a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots do the physical cutting. The children may be grown, but I won't assume the mortgage is paid or my partner's grocery hours are unchanged. Four months saved gives us a choice if there are still paid shifts and some local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the cutter job and use new overtime wages, when offered, to pay extra on the mortgage after bills. I'll ask my cousin, a furniture maker, for the names of workshops offering real paid guarded apprenticeships, then check the posted terms myself. If a funded paid trim course with a supervised place is offered, I'll enrol; if my cutter hours later fall, I'll apply after qualifying for posted safe local workshop jobs only if base pay and travel fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far-off change, but our current wages give me time to ask. I would rather learn on a real bench than guess about a robot brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your cousin really find out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin can tell me which shop teaches an apprentice and which just needs cheap labour. My furniture-maker cousin cannot promise a paid apprenticeship seat. I would ask the employer for the fee, training wage and guard arrangements in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make workshop work worth moving to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A workshop job must show its regular pay and an actual shift that lets us manage family errands. If it requires an hour of travel each way for lower wages, I would keep the cutter shift while I looked elsewhere. The title alone does not make a job fit.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes cut lists before robots handle foam around 2039.
A **real apprenticeship** needs a paid place and supervised guarded work.
think: At **56**, I may still need a wage for the mortgage.
The **four-month reserve** helps choose if current shifts continue.
do: **Pay** extra mortgage principal from new offered overtime after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded trim training if a supervised place opens.
**Apply** for posted safe local workshop jobs if qualified, hours cut, pay and travel fit.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robots with current wages intact.
S4.quote: My furniture-maker cousin cannot promise a paid apprenticeship seat.
fieldNote: His **family contact** supplies workshop names but cannot promise a course seat or paid job.
The **workshop application** remains tied to qualification, actual cutter cuts and a local posted role at workable pay and travel.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from offered paid overtime after bills
Ask furniture-maker cousin for workshops with paid guarded apprenticeships
Enrol in trim course if funded paid guarded supervised place offered
Apply for posted safe local workshop role if qualified, hours cut, pay and travel fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove most cutter shifts before I have another paid trade. Written notice, offered paid practical instruction and posted safe local work at a wage that covers the mortgage would help. I would talk it through with my partner before moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who measures the first mattress panel after a robot changes a blade. A crooked foam cut becomes someone else's bad night's sleep.

headlineQuote: A crooked foam cut becomes someone else's bad night's sleep.
portrait: **Colin**, 43, operates a mattress foam cutter with a vocational certificate, ordinary pay and four months saved.
He and his grocery-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with some similar plants nearby.
His **traditional outlook** favors paid instruction from family and workshop trades; he never uses AI tools.
Fast robots make him **alarmed** about lost cutter wages, while longer warnings allow careful paid apprenticeship and vacancy checks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable foam-cutting robots around 2031 and remove most mortgage-paying shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, offered paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient regular pay would help.
